standard.title: Causes of British colonies after 1800
standard.description: the economic, political and social causes of the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4K02 (Causes of the first British colony): Students explain the causes of the establishment of the first British colony in Australia.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the economic, political and social causes of the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800, distinguishing between different colony types and the reasons for each.

nodes.label: Types of colonies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that different types of British colonies were established in Australia after 1800, including penal colonies and colonies for free settlers, and name examples of each.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two types of colonies (penal and free settler) and provide one example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Distinguish between penal colonies (e.g. Moreton Bay, Van Diemen's Land) and free settler colonies (e.g. South Australia, Victoria), explaining the intended purpose of each.
wider: Investigate how the type of colony influenced its early social structure, laws and treatment of First Nations Australians in that location
Explore how colony type shaped the economy and land use practices in the early decades of settlement
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't distinguish colony types will conflate the economic, political and social causes that follow — causes were not uniform across all colonies. The distinctions underpin all subsequent causal reasoning.

response_modes.reason: Use sorting activities (e.g. card sorts by colony type) and explicit classification frameworks to ensure students can categorise examples before moving to causes.

success_criteria: Students identify at least two types of British colonies and give a named example of each.
Students explain the intended purpose of each colony type in one or two sentences.

nodes.label: Economic causes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain economic reasons for the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800, including acquisition of land and resources, and economic conditions in Britain.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one economic cause (e.g. land and resource acquisition or economic hardship in Britain).
nodes.typical_width: Explain the range of economic causes: acquisition of land and resources, high unemployment and poverty in Britain, and the economic potential of Australian land for farming and resource extraction.
wider: Investigate how global trade interests and competition between European powers shaped British economic motivations for colonisation
Examine the role of specific industries (e.g. wool, whaling, grain) in the economic argument for expanding Australian colonies

response_modes.reason: Economic causes are best understood by comparing the British economic context with the colonial opportunity — use both perspectives to deepen understanding rather than a single causal story.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The relationship between British economic conditions and colonial resource opportunity is a genuinely productive site for historical thinking — students can explore global trade context and the specific industries that shaped colony locations.
success_criteria: Students name at least two economic causes and explain how each contributed to establishing colonies.
Students connect British economic conditions (e.g. unemployment, overcrowding) to the decision to colonise.

nodes.label: Political causes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain political reasons for the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800, including expanding the British Empire and strategic concerns about competing nations.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one political cause (e.g. expanding the British Empire).
nodes.typical_width: Explain that political causes included expanding the British Empire's global reach and concern that other colonial powers (e.g. France) might claim Australian territory.
wider: Investigate the geopolitical context of European colonialism in the late 18th and 19th centuries, comparing British motivations with those of France and other powers
Explore how colonial policy was influenced by British parliamentary politics and competing interests within British government

response_modes.reason: Political causes become more meaningful when set against the broader European colonial context — comparative framing helps students see British motives as deliberate strategic choices rather than inevitable events.

success_criteria: Students explain at least one political cause and link it to a decision to establish a specific colony or expand settlement.
Students distinguish political causes from economic and social causes.

nodes.label: Social causes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain social reasons for the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800, including overcrowded British cities, high crime rates and overflowing prisons.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one social cause (e.g. overcrowded British prisons).
nodes.typical_width: Explain the range of social causes: overcrowded cities, high crime rates, overflowing prisons, and the use of transportation as a solution to Britain's social problems.
wider: Investigate the lives of transported convicts — who they were, their crimes, and their experiences of the voyage and arrival in the colony
Examine First Nations Australian perspectives on the arrival of convicts and settlers as a social and cultural disruption to established ways of life

response_modes.reason: Social causes are most vivid when explored through case studies of real transported individuals — concrete human stories ground abstract social conditions in ways that support understanding.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations perspectives on colonisation are a pedagogically significant and elaboration-supported wider direction that adds genuine breadth — this is not just more British social history but a distinct cultural and historical lens.
success_criteria: Students name at least two social causes and explain how they contributed to transportation and colonisation.
Students explain the connection between social conditions in Britain and the decision to use Australia for transportation.

nodes.label: Integrating multiple causes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the economic, political and social causes of the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800, identifying how different causes applied to different colony types.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least one cause from each category (economic, political, social) and link each to the establishment of at least one colony.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the full range of economic, political and social causes, distinguishing how different causes applied more strongly to penal versus free settler colonies, and identify which causes were most significant.
wider: Construct a comparative analysis of two different colonies, examining how the combination of causes shaped the character of each colony differently
Evaluate which category of cause (economic, political or social) was most significant overall, using evidence from multiple colonies to support the argument

response_modes.reason: The integration node requires students to bring all three cause categories together into a coherent explanation. Use structured tasks such as cause-and-effect matrices or comparative colony profiles to support this synthesis.

success_criteria: Students explain at least one economic, one political and one social cause in an integrated account.
Students show how the mix of causes differed between at least two colony types.
Students' explanation uses relevant historical terminology (e.g. 'penal colony', 'free settlers', 'transportation').
